stem: A company is moving an HTTP web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Business partners call the application from their own networks over the internet. The company needs one entry point in front of the instances that keeps serving requests when an instance fails. Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
keywords: Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule that forwards /api/* requests to a second target group and all other requests to the first target group.
options.why: Path conditions let the load balancer [forward requests based on the URL](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-path-conditions-smaller-services), so /api/* requests reach their own target group through one load balancer.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet and a TCP listener that forwards all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and picks a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection), so it cannot send /api/* requests to a separate group.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register as its target an Application Load Balancer that has a /api/* listener rule.
options.why: It works, but the company pays for two load balancers, and each one is billed for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) that it runs.

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic IP address with its node in each subnet, and forward all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

explanation: The load balancer has to read the URL of each request. An Application Load Balancer [functions at the application layer](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-layer-7), and a listener rule with a [path-pattern](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-condition-types) condition sends /api/* requests to a second target group. One load balancer does the whole job, so it is also the cheapest design.
takeaway: Routing by URL path needs Application Load Balancer listener rules, and one ALB can serve several target groups.
twin: If the stem said "the addresses must never change" instead: a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses, because you can [optionally associate one Elastic IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip) for each zone.
say: The /api rule needs layer 7, so one Application Load Balancer with a second target group is the answer.

stem: A solutions architect reviews the design of a new internet-facing TCP application on Amazon EC2 instances. In the design, a Network Load Balancer has one subnet, in Availability Zone A, and all the instances run in Availability Zone A. The application must be highly available and must keep serving clients if one Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: one subnet, in Availability Zone A
all the instances run in Availability Zone A

options.text: Replace the instances in Availability Zone A with larger instance types so that the remaining instances can carry the load when one instance fails.
options.why: Larger instances still run in one zone, so the loss of Availability Zone A still stops the whole application.

options.text: Give the Network Load Balancer a subnet in Availability Zone B as well, so that it has a load balancer node in each of the two zones.
options.why: When you enable a zone, Elastic Load Balancing [creates a load balancer node](../facts/elb.md#elb-node-per-enabled-az) there, so clients keep an entry point if Availability Zone A fails.

options.text: Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group so that the load balancer node in Availability Zone A can also use targets in other zones.
options.why: Cross-zone load balancing uses the [registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does), and here one zone is enabled and holds every instance.
options.misconception: believes that cross-zone load balancing reaches zones that the load balancer does not have

options.text: Run instances in Availability Zone B as well, for example with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones and registers its instances with the target group.
options.why: AWS asks you to [avoid single points of failure, including the underlying physical infrastructure](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-rel10-bp01-avoid-single-points-of-failure); instances in a second zone do that for the targets.

options.text: Create a second Network Load Balancer with a subnet in Availability Zone B, and use Amazon Route 53 failover records to switch clients between the two load balancers.
options.why: It works with instances in both zones, but it adds a second load balancer and DNS failover records, where one load balancer with two zones does the same.

explanation: If Availability Zone A fails, everything in it stops, so the load balancer and the targets both need a second zone. When a zone has no healthy target, the Network Load Balancer removes the address of the [corresponding subnet from DNS](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-unhealthy-az-removed-from-dns-fail-open), and clients reach the node in the healthy zone.
takeaway: To survive a zone failure, the load balancer needs a node and healthy targets in a second zone.
twin: If the stem said "the instances already run in both zones" instead: enable the second zone alone, because until then [these registered targets do not receive traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-in-disabled-az-no-traffic).
say: A load balancer in one zone is still one zone, so add a second zone to the load balancer and put instances there.

stem: A company runs an API on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one VPC. Listener rules send /orders/* and /reports/* to separate target groups. A large customer now requires a fixed set of IP addresses that it can allow-list in its firewall. The path-based routing must stay in place, and the company uses one AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: requires a fixed set of IP addresses
The path-based routing must stay in place

options.text: Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer that has an Elastic IP address in each subnet, and move the path rules to its listener.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and picks a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection), so it has no /orders/* or /reports/* path rules.

options.text: Associate an Elastic IP address with the Application Load Balancer node in each subnet, and give the customer those addresses to allow-list.
options.why: The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register the existing Application Load Balancer as its target.
options.why: To give ALB routing fixed addresses, you [forward traffic from your Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-static-ip-privatelink) to it, and the ALB [takes over the load balancing decision](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-combines-features).

options.text: Launch Amazon EC2 instances with Elastic IP addresses that run reverse proxy software, and have them forward every request to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: It works, but the company has to patch, scale and replace the proxy instances itself, where a managed Network Load Balancer does the same job.

explanation: The customer needs fixed addresses, and the API still needs rules that read the URL. A Network Load Balancer gives [static IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-static-ip-privatelink) and forwards to an ALB-type target group, where the ALB keeps its path rules. Both load balancers must be [in the same VPC](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-same-vpc-same-account), which the stem gives.
takeaway: Fixed IP addresses plus path rules: put a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses in front of the ALB.
twin: If the stem said "the company uses two AWS Regions" instead: AWS Global Accelerator, because it gives [static IP addresses that serve as fixed endpoints](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-global-accelerator-static-ips) for [load balancers in one or more AWS Regions](../facts/elb.md#elb-ga-alb-multiple-regions).
say: Keep the Application Load Balancer for the path rules, and put a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses in front of it.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: the customer needs a fixed set of IP addresses, the /orders/* and /reports/* path rules must stay, and everything runs in one VPC in one Region.
Before I look at the options, I predict a swap: replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer, because the Network Load Balancer is the type with static and Elastic IP addresses.

I remove the Elastic IP addresses on the Application Load Balancer nodes, because the feature table gives static and Elastic IP addresses to the Network Load Balancer only. I remove the proxy instances, because the company would have to run and patch them.

Between the swap and a Network Load Balancer in front of the Application Load Balancer, the difference is the path rules. My first idea breaks because a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and picks a target with a flow hash, so the path rules would be lost. The stem says the rules must stay, so I keep the Application Load Balancer as the target of the Network Load Balancer.
Check: the Elastic IP addresses stay fixed, the Application Load Balancer keeps its rules, and both load balancers sit in the same VPC of one account. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company hosts three websites, example.com, example.net and example.org, on Amazon EC2 instances behind one Application Load Balancer. Host-based listener rules send the requests of each website to its own target group. The company must now encrypt the traffic in transit between users and the load balancer, and every website must stay on port 443. Each website has its own public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: every website must stay on port 443

options.text: Create HTTPS listeners on ports 443, 8443 and 9443, one per website, and attach that website's ACM certificate to each.
options.why: Every website must stay on port 443, and one listener can serve them all, because a certificate list can [provide a different certificate for each domain](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).

options.text: Create three Application Load Balancers, one per website, each with an HTTPS listener on port 443 and that website's ACM certificate.
options.why: It works, but three load balancers mean three charges for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) and three listeners to manage, where one listener is enough.

options.text: Replace the load balancer with a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, and install each website's certificate on the instances.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type), so the host-based rules are lost, and every instance then needs its own certificates.
options.misconception: moves TLS to the instances and expects the host-based rules to keep working

options.text: Create one HTTPS listener on port 443, and add all three ACM certificates to the certificate list of that listener.
options.why: A certificate list lets one listener [support multiple domains on the same port](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains) and choose with a [smart certificate selection algorithm with support for SNI](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).

explanation: The three names have different parent domains, so one wildcard certificate does not cover them. One HTTPS listener holds a default certificate plus a certificate list, and [SNI is automatically enabled](../facts/elb.md#elb-faq-sni-automatic-multiple-certificates) when the listener has [more than one TLS certificate](../facts/elb.md#elb-faq-sni-automatic-multiple-certificates). The load balancer reads the host name that the client sends and presents the matching certificate.
takeaway: Several HTTPS domains on one port: one listener with a certificate list, and SNI picks the certificate.
twin: If the stem said "shop.example.com, help.example.com and news.example.com" instead: one certificate could cover all three, because you can [use a wildcard certificate](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cert-wildcard-or-san-single-cert).
say: One HTTPS listener takes a list of certificates, and SNI picks the right one for each host name.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.

I mark the constraints: three websites with different parent domains, host rules on one load balancer, encryption in transit to the load balancer, port 443 for every website, and one ACM certificate for each website.

Before I look at the options, I predict one HTTPS listener on port 443 with all three certificates, because a certificate list lets one listener serve several domains on the same port, and SNI picks the certificate.
I remove the listeners on ports 8443 and 9443, because every website must stay on port 443. I remove the Network Load Balancer, because it works at layer 4 and would lose the host rules.

Between the certificate list and three load balancers, the difference is how many resources the team runs and pays for; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, and each load balancer is billed by the hour, so one listener with a certificate list wins.
Check: the certificate list keeps port 443, keeps the host rules and uses the three ACM certificates. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances that are registered in an Application Load Balancer target group with the default health check settings. After a release, the application currently answers requests for the path / with an HTTP 302 redirect to a sign-in page. Every target is now marked unhealthy, but users can still use the website. The company must ensure that the health checks show the real state of each target. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Every target is now marked unhealthy, but users can still use the website

options.text: Make no change, because the load balancer stops sending requests to unhealthy targets, so the health checks already protect the users.
options.why: With every target unhealthy, [the load balancer fails open](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy) and [routes requests to all those targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy), so the checks protect nobody.

options.text: Change the health check protocol of the target group to TCP so that a target counts as healthy when it accepts a connection.
options.why: For an Application Load Balancer health check, [the possible protocols are HTTP and HTTPS](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-protocol-default-http), so a TCP check is not an option.
options.misconception: believes that an Application Load Balancer target group can use a TCP health check

options.text: Change the health check path of the target group to a /health page that returns HTTP 200 when the application can serve requests.
options.why: The check passes on the success code, and [the default value is 200](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200); a /health page that returns 200 passes while the application works.

options.text: Change the application so that the path / returns HTTP 200 instead of a redirect, and release the new version to every instance.
options.why: It works, but it changes application code and needs a new release, where one target group setting fixes the check.

explanation: The health check requests the path /, and for the success code [the default value is 200](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200). The application now answers / with 302, so every check fails. Users still get pages because, with every target unhealthy at once, [the load balancer fails open](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy). A /health path that returns 200 makes the check report the real state of each target.
takeaway: All targets unhealthy but the site still works: the ALB failed open, so fix the health check path or success codes.
twin: If the stem said "the team cannot add a new path to the application" instead: add 302 to the success codes, which can be [200 to 499](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200).
say: The check expects 200 and gets a 302, so point it at a health page; the load balancer only failed open.

stem: A company runs a three-tier application in one VPC. The internet-facing web tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances, and users must reach it through one endpoint. The web tier calls the application tier, which also runs on EC2 instances. Each tier must scale on its own. The application tier must be reachable privately from the web tier and must stay unreachable from the internet. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must be reachable privately from the web tier
Each tier must scale on its own

options.text: Add a listener rule to the internet-facing load balancer that forwards /app/* requests to a target group of the application tier instances.
options.why: A path rule on the internet-facing load balancer lets any user on the internet reach the application tier with a /app/* request.
options.misconception: believes that a path rule keeps a tier hidden from the internet

options.text: Give the application tier instances public IP addresses in public subnets so that the internet-facing load balancer can reach them as targets.
options.why: Targets are reached [using private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-need-no-public-ip), so public addresses only add exposure for the application tier.

options.text: Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in public subnets, and register the web tier instances in its target group.
options.why: Its nodes [have public IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internet-facing-nodes-public-ips) and accept users from the internet, and the web instances behind it can stay in private subnets.

options.text: Launch Amazon EC2 instances that run open source proxy software in private subnets, and have them spread the web tier's calls over the application tier.
options.why: It works, but the company has to run, patch and scale the proxy instances itself, which an internal load balancer avoids.

options.text: Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets, register the application tier instances, and point the web tier's calls at it.
options.why: Internal nodes [have only private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only), so only [clients with access to the VPC](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only) reach the application tier.

explanation: AWS describes this pattern for multi-tier applications, with [both internal and internet-facing load balancers](../facts/elb.md#elb-multi-tier-internet-facing-plus-internal). The web instances register with the internet-facing load balancer and send their calls to the internal one, which forwards them to the application tier. Each tier scales behind its own load balancer, and the application tier has no public entry point.
takeaway: A private tier behind a public tier: an internet-facing load balancer for the web tier and an internal one for the application tier.
twin: If the stem said "partners on the internet also call the application tier" instead: the application tier needs an internet-facing load balancer too, because internal nodes [have only private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only).
say: Users reach an internet-facing load balancer, and the web tier calls an internal one that only the VPC can reach.

stem: A company runs a TCP service on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer that was created with default settings. The instances run across multiple Availability Zones: 2 instances in Availability Zone A and 6 instances in Availability Zone B. Client connections are spread evenly over the two load balancer nodes. The 2 instances in Availability Zone A are overloaded, and the other instances are mostly idle. The company must spread connections evenly over all 8 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Client connections are spread evenly over the two load balancer nodes

options.text: Add 2 instances in each Availability Zone, because cross-zone load balancing is already turned on for every type of load balancer.
options.why: On a Network Load Balancer, [cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-gwlb-cross-zone-off-by-default), so each node still uses the instances of its own zone, and the load stays uneven.

options.text: Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group, and accept the charge for data that crosses between Availability Zones.
options.why: Each node then uses the [registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does), and the data is [charged for regional data transfer between Availability Zones](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-faq-cross-zone-regional-data-transfer-charged).

options.text: Change the routing algorithm of the target group to least outstanding requests so that new connections go to the least busy instances.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer selects a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection); [least outstanding requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-routing-algorithms-three) is an algorithm of Application Load Balancer target groups.
options.misconception: believes that a Network Load Balancer target group has the routing algorithms of an Application Load Balancer

options.text: Launch 4 more instances in Availability Zone A, and keep the same number of instances in each zone whenever the fleet changes size.
options.why: It works, but the team has to keep both zones equal at every change, where one setting spreads connections over all instances.

explanation: With cross-zone load balancing off, each node uses the [registered targets in its Availability Zone](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does). The two nodes get the same number of connections, so each of the 2 instances in Availability Zone A carries three times the load of an instance in Availability Zone B. On a Network Load Balancer you can turn cross-zone load balancing [on or off at the target group level](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-cross-zone-lb-and-tg-level).
takeaway: Uneven instance counts per zone behind an NLB: turn on cross-zone load balancing and pay for the data between zones.
twin: If the stem said "an Application Load Balancer" instead: no change is needed, because cross-zone load balancing is [on by default](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cross-zone-on-by-default) for it.
say: Cross-zone is off by default on a Network Load Balancer, so turn it on and accept the data transfer charge.

stem: A company runs a file upload service on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Some uploads are long-running and take up to 10 minutes. The target group uses the default deregistration delay. When the group scales in, some uploads that are still in progress on the instances that the group removes fail. The company wants minimal downtime for uploads during scale-in. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Increase the idle timeout of the load balancer to 900 seconds so that connections to the instances stay open during scale-in.
options.why: The idle timeout ends connections that stay idle; its default is [60 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-idle-timeout-default-60-seconds), and an upload that sends data is not idle.
options.misconception: confuses the idle timeout of a connection with the wait for in-flight requests during deregistration

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions for the target group so that each user's upload stays on the same instance until the upload is complete.
options.why: Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), but they do not delay the deregistration of that target during scale-in.
options.misconception: believes that stickiness keeps an instance in service until its users finish

options.text: Add a lifecycle hook to the Auto Scaling group, and run a script on each instance that completes the hook after its uploads finish.
options.why: It works, but the team has to write and maintain a script on every instance, where one target group setting waits for the uploads.

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay of the target group to 900 seconds so that in-progress uploads can finish before an instance is removed.
options.why: Deregistration lets the load balancer [help in-flight requests to the target to complete](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-deregistration-waits-for-in-flight), and the delay accepts [0 to 3600 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds), which covers a 10-minute upload.

explanation: During scale-in, the load balancer [stops routing requests to a target](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregister-stops-routing-draining) that is deregistering and waits [until in-flight requests have completed](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregister-stops-routing-draining), for at most the deregistration delay. After that, [it can be terminated and replaced](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-deregistration-draining-then-unused). The delay is [300 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds) by default, shorter than a 10-minute upload.
takeaway: Requests cut off during scale-in: raise the deregistration delay of the target group above the longest request.
twin: If the stem said "take up to 2 minutes" instead: no change is needed, because the default delay of [300 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds) already covers the uploads.
say: Raise the deregistration delay above the longest upload, so draining waits for the uploads before the instance goes away.

stem: A company's website runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The HTTPS listener uses a certificate that a third-party certificate authority issued and that the company imported into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Last year the certificate expired, and the website was unavailable until an engineer imported a new certificate. The company wants to automate certificate renewal so that this outage does not happen again. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep the imported certificate on the listener, and rely on ACM managed renewal to renew the certificate before it expires.
options.why: ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for imported certificates, so the company still has to renew this one itself.

options.text: Upload the third-party certificate to IAM, and change the HTTPS listener to use the IAM certificate instead of the ACM certificate.
options.why: You can [upload the certificate](../facts/acm.md#acm-alb-certificate-from-acm-or-iam) to IAM, but that changes where it is stored, not who renews it; the company still renews it.
options.misconception: believes that a certificate in IAM renews itself

options.text: Request a public certificate for the domain from ACM, and replace the imported certificate on the HTTPS listener with it.
options.why: Certificates provided by ACM and deployed on the load balancer [can be renewed automatically](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically), and renewal [does not affect in-flight requests](../facts/acm.md#acm-alb-renewal-in-flight).

options.text: Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that buys a new certificate from the third-party authority every year and imports it into ACM.
options.why: It works, but the company has to write and fix code that buys and imports certificates, where an ACM certificate renews itself.

explanation: The outage came from a manual step. For an imported certificate, ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal), and [you must monitor the expiration date](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically). A certificate that ACM issues and deploys on the load balancer [can be renewed automatically](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically), and new requests then use the renewed certificate.
takeaway: ACM renews the certificates it issues, not the ones you import; use an ACM certificate to automate renewal.
twin: If the stem said "the company must keep its current certificate authority" instead: a scheduled re-import becomes the answer, because ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for imported certificates.
say: ACM does not renew an imported certificate, so request one from ACM and let ACM renew it.

stem: A company has several VPCs in one AWS Region and a central security VPC. Security policy requires that all traffic into and out of each VPC passes through a fleet of third-party firewall appliances that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The fleet must be scalable as traffic grows, and the company wants to centrally manage the appliances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: all traffic into and out of each VPC

options.text: Create a Gateway Load Balancer for the appliances in the security VPC, add Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in each VPC, and route traffic to the endpoints.
options.why: With endpoints, the appliances [can reside in different AWS accounts and VPCs](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-endpoint-centralize-appliances), and each route table sends traffic to an endpoint [as the next hop in the route table](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-endpoint-next-hop-route-table).

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer for the appliances in the security VPC, and point every client and application at the DNS name of that load balancer.
options.why: Traffic between other hosts is not sent to the load balancer's name, so it bypasses the appliances; inline appliances need a load balancer that is [invisible to the source and destination](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances).

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer with an AWS WAF web ACL in each VPC, and send all inbound web requests through that load balancer.
options.why: AWS WAF can [block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-waf-integrates-with-alb) to the load balancer, but the policy requires third-party appliances for all traffic of each VPC.
options.misconception: treats a web application firewall for HTTP requests as inspection of all traffic

options.text: Create a separate Gateway Load Balancer and a separate fleet of appliances in each VPC, and route the traffic of each VPC through its own fleet.
options.why: It works, but a load balancer and a fleet in every VPC multiply the appliances to patch and scale, where endpoints share one central fleet.

explanation: The traffic is not addressed to the appliances, so this is a Gateway Load Balancer case: it is for [deploying inline virtual appliances](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) and [transparently passes all Layer 3 traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) through them. Endpoints in each VPC receive the traffic from route tables, and the appliances stay [centralized in one location](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-endpoint-centralize-appliances).
takeaway: All traffic through third-party appliances, steered by route tables: a Gateway Load Balancer with endpoints in each VPC.
twin: If the stem said "filter the HTTP requests to the company's web application" instead: an Application Load Balancer with an AWS WAF web ACL, because it can [block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-waf-integrates-with-alb).
say: Inline firewalls mean a Gateway Load Balancer, and route tables send each VPC's traffic to its endpoint.

stem: A company is moving an HTTP web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Business partners call the application from their own networks over the internet. The company needs one entry point in front of the instances that keeps serving requests when an instance fails. Each partner must allow-list the load balancer's IP addresses, and the addresses must never change. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
keywords: allow-list the load balancer's IP addresses

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule that forwards /api/* requests to a second target group and all other requests to the first target group.
options.why: Elastic Load Balancing [scales your load balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap) and keeps a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap) on its DNS entry, so the [IP addresses can be remapped quickly](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap).

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet and a TCP listener that forwards all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: The Network Load Balancer creates a network interface in each enabled zone and [uses it to get a static IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip); here it is an Elastic IP address.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register as its target an Application Load Balancer that has a /api/* listener rule.
options.why: It gives fixed addresses too, but the extra Application Load Balancer adds a second charge for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour).

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic IP address with its node in each subnet, and forward all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

explanation: The partners need fixed addresses. In the AWS feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) belongs to the Network Load Balancer. With Elastic IP addresses, its addresses [must be completely controlled by you](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-faq-no-mix-eip-and-elb-ips), so the [addresses known to your clients do not change](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-faq-no-mix-eip-and-elb-ips). No HTTP routing is needed, so one load balancer is enough.
takeaway: Fixed IP addresses for a partner allow-list point to a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses.
twin: If the stem said "Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances" instead: an Application Load Balancer with a path rule, because it can [forward requests based on the URL](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-path-conditions-smaller-services).
say: Partners need fixed addresses, so a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses; an ALB's addresses change.
